## My pick: a commitment ledger

The thing only Plaud can do, that nothing else in your stack can, is hear what you *say you'll do*. Your calendar knows what you scheduled. Things 3 knows what you typed in. But the promises live in the air. "I'll call my mom this weekend." "We should grab coffee soon." "I really need to finish that cover letter." "Yeah, I'll send you that link." Those evaporate the second the conversation ends, and the gap between what you say and what you do is exactly where things fall through the cracks.

So: an agent that listens to every transcript, extracts every commitment you voice (to others *and* to yourself), and then checks reality to see if it happened. It cross-references your calendar, your tasks, and your *later* transcripts. Then it surfaces the gap. "You've now said you'll set up that coffee with Eleanor three separate times across two weeks. Want me to just send the text?"

This is the most uniquely-Plaud idea I can think of, and it's the literal embodiment of the accountability-partner job. It's also a clean 10-day build: ingest, extract, match against reality, surface. And this is where "unlimited credits" actually matters, because day one you'd re-process your *entire* back catalog (350-ish transcripts) to seed the ledger, then run continuous extraction going forward. The demo writes itself: "Here are the 23 things you committed to last month. 14 happened. Here are the 9 that didn't, ranked by how many times you've re-promised them."

## The substrate it sits on

To build that well, you'd first need two things that are also valuable on their own:

1. **Semantic search over everything you've ever said.** Index every transcript into a vector store so you can ask "what did the roofer quote me?" or "what was that book Eleanor recommended?" and get the answer from your own spoken life. Right now those memories are gone. This is the foundation the ledger queries against.

2. **Speaker attribution.** If the API exposes diarization, every conversation gets rolled into a per-person memory. Then before you see someone, you get a brief: last time you talked, they mentioned their daughter's recital, they were stressed about work, you promised to send them a link. That's your CRM, but populated automatically from real talk instead of you logging it. (Caveat: this one depends on what the API actually gives you. If there's no speaker labeling, it gets harder, so I'd treat it as the stretch goal.)

So the shape is: build the searchable spoken-memory substrate, then the commitment ledger is the hero app on top, and the relationship briefs are the second app if diarization is there.

## Two other directions, if you want a different flavor

- **The longitudinal mirror.** Run analysis across months of transcripts to show you yourself: what topics keep recurring, who you talk about most, where your stated values drift from your actions, how your energy reads over time.
